lessons.title: The three roles at a glance

blocks.text: The job changes from writing the best code to making the best decisions, and then to making other people's decisions better.

rows: One team and its roadmap (4–8 engineers)
All of mobile, plus the backend and platform contracts it depends on
One or more teams, then the whole mobile org (8–40+ people)
Quality and delivery of your own work
The team's delivery, quality and technical health
Technical direction, architecture and engineering standards
People, hiring, performance, delivery commitments and team structure
Quarter to two years, plus each person's career
20–40%, mostly prototypes, critical paths and reviews
Strong teams, hires, promotions, plans that are met
The team ships predictably without heroics
The org ships faster and safer because of choices you drove
The org delivers, people grow and stay, and leaders trust your commitments

blocks.text: Principal Engineer and Engineering Manager are parallel tracks in most ladders, not rungs of one ladder. PE is the senior individual-contributor path; EM is the people-management path. Moving from PE to EM is a change of job, usually at the same level. Confirm your company's own ladder document with your manager: titles and expectations differ between companies.

lessons.title: SSE to Tech Lead: what to start doing now

blocks.text: You get the TL role by doing the TL job on a small scale before the title arrives. Ask your manager directly what gap they see between you and TL, and get it in writing.
**Take ownership of an outcome, not a ticket**

items: Volunteer to lead one multi-sprint project end to end: scoping, design doc, task breakdown, risk tracking, release and post-launch metrics.
Own one area fully, for example checkout and payments, so that product and QA come to you first.
Report status before anyone asks. A weekly three-line update (done, next, risks) builds more trust than any single feature.
Review code for design and risk, and explain the reasoning so the author learns.
Mentor one or two engineers with a regular 1:1 and a concrete growth goal for each.
Write down what only you know: onboarding notes, architecture overview, method-channel conventions between Flutter and native iOS.
Write a design doc for every non-trivial change: problem, options considered, decision, risks, rollout and rollback.
Estimate with ranges and state assumptions. Flag slippage early with a proposed fix.
Learn the business numbers your features move: conversion, order value, crash-free sessions, app start time.

blocks.text: **Evidence to collect for the promotion case**

rows: Led a project with other engineers
Three-person feature delivered on the planned date with a staged rollout
Design doc adopted by the team, with the measured result
An engineer who now owns a module independently
Crash rate, build time or release cycle before and after
Feedback from product, design, QA and backend partners

lessons.title: Running a mobile team as Tech Lead

blocks.text: A Tech Lead's week has four jobs: keep delivery predictable, keep the codebase healthy, grow the people, and protect release quality.

items: Break every project into milestones of two weeks or less, each with something demonstrable.
Keep a visible risk list with an owner and a date for each item.
Put new behaviour behind feature flags and remote config so that a release never depends on one unfinished feature.
Reserve 15–20% of each sprint for tech debt and tooling, agreed with product in advance.
Set the team's conventions once and automate them: lint rules, state management pattern, module boundaries, PR template.
Record significant decisions as short Architecture Decision Records so that the reasoning survives team changes.
Delegate design work on purpose. Your job is to review designs, not to write all of them.
Hold a 1:1 with each engineer every one to two weeks. Cover blockers, growth and feedback in both directions.
Match work to growth: give stretch tasks with a safety net, and avoid giving the hardest work to yourself.
Give feedback within a few days, specific to one behaviour and its effect.
Take part in hiring: interview, calibrate, and own onboarding for new joiners.
Own the release train: fixed cadence, branch cut, regression, staged rollout (for example 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%), and clear halt criteria.
Watch crash-free rate, ANRs, app start time and key funnel conversion for each release before widening the rollout.
Run a blameless review after every production incident and track the actions to closure.

lessons.title: Tech Lead to Principal Engineer: org-wide leverage

blocks.text: A Principal Engineer is judged on problems solved across teams that no single team would have solved alone. A strong TL who only makes one team excellent stays a TL.

items: Look for pain that repeats in several teams: slow builds, flaky tests, duplicated UI components, inconsistent networking and caching, painful Flutter–native bridging, release delays.
Rank them by cost to the business, in engineer-hours lost, incidents or revenue at risk.
Pick one or two. Depth on a few large problems counts more than a long list of small fixes.
Write a mobile technical strategy of two to four pages: where the apps are today, the main problems, the target state in 12–24 months, and the order of work.
Run an RFC process so that decisions that affect several teams get reviewed by those teams.
Take clear positions on the questions that keep returning: Flutter versus native for a given surface, modularisation, design system ownership, server-driven UI, offline behaviour.
Meet each mobile lead and the backend, QA, design and product heads regularly. Know their top two problems.
Build agreement one conversation at a time before the review meeting.
Sponsor other engineers to lead parts of your initiatives. Their growth is part of your result.
Keep writing code on the hardest and riskiest parts: proofs of concept, performance investigations, migration tooling.
Lead the response to the worst incidents and the deep investigations that follow.
Track platform changes early: new iOS and Android releases, Flutter stable releases, store policy changes, and what they cost the org.
Tie every proposal to a business measure: conversion, retention, order frequency, delivery cost or engineering cost.
Present options with cost, benefit and risk so that leadership can choose.

lessons.title: Principal Engineer to Engineering Manager: the track change

blocks.text: Moving to EM means giving up technical ownership in exchange for responsibility for people. It is a new job that you start as a beginner, and your PE-level credibility is what makes the team accept you in it.

rows: Fastest; most EM openings are filled this way
Less technical depth; harder to lead senior engineers and argue architecture
Deep credibility; you can manage PEs and own technical strategy as a senior EM or head of mobile
Longer; PE roles are few; you must unlearn solving problems yourself

blocks.text: Both are valid. If EM is the fixed goal, tell your manager now so that people-management opportunities come to you during the TL years, whichever route you take.

rows: You make or shape the technical decision
You make sure a good decision gets made, by the right owner
Success is visible in designs and systems
Success is visible in other people's results, months later
A calendar of 1:1s, reviews, planning and hiring
You can say what you think of a design
Your opinion carries rating power, so you speak last
Peers are other managers, product heads and HR partners

items: Manage two to four people for at least two review cycles while still TL or PE.
Run a full hiring loop: write the job description, screen, interview, debrief, close the offer.
Handle one hard people situation with your manager's coaching: underperformance, a conflict or a resignation.
Shadow your manager in planning, calibration and headcount discussions.
Ask yourself after six months whether a day with no code and a solved people problem felt like a good day. If not, PE is the better destination.
Days 1–30: listen. Hold a long 1:1 with every report. Ask what is working, what is broken and what they want from their career. Change nothing large.
Days 31–60: name a technical owner (TL or PE) for everything you used to own. Fix two or three small things people asked for. Share your operating rhythm in writing.
Days 61–90: publish team goals for the next two quarters, a hiring plan, and a growth plan for each person.

lessons.title: Running the mobile org as Engineering Manager

blocks.text: An EM's output is the output of the organisation. The work falls into seven areas.

items: Hold a 30–45 minute 1:1 with every direct report weekly or fortnightly. Their agenda comes first.
Keep a private note per person: goals, feedback given, commitments made, signs of low morale.
Agree a written growth plan with each person every half-year: target level, two or three gaps, the projects that will close them.
Keep direct reports to about five to eight. Above that, add a lead layer.
Set expectations in writing against the ladder at the start of each cycle.
Give feedback continuously so that the review contains no surprises.
Prepare for calibration with evidence: scope, results, peer feedback, comparison with the level definition.
Act on underperformance within weeks: name the gap, agree a dated improvement plan, review weekly, involve HR early.
Build promotion cases six months ahead and find the missing evidence with the person.
Own the headcount plan: which roles, which levels, which quarter, and the justification.
Design a consistent loop: coding, mobile system design, platform depth (Flutter, iOS or Android), and a values and collaboration round.
Train interviewers and hold a debrief with written feedback submitted before discussion.
Run a 30-60-90 day onboarding plan with a buddy and a first production change in week one.
Watch retention signals: stalled growth, pay gaps, repeated on-call load, loss of a close colleague. Hold stay conversations before exit conversations.
Run quarterly planning with product: capacity, committed items, stretch items, and a tech-investment share of 15–25%.
Track commitments made against commitments met, and explain misses with causes.
Manage dependencies with backend, design, QA and other mobile teams in a single visible plan.
Protect the team from mid-sprint changes; route new requests through a known intake.
Shape teams around business areas (for example discovery, cart and checkout, payments, orders and delivery) with a platform team for shared code.
Give each team a TL, a clear charter and named module ownership.
Decide where Flutter, iOS and Android specialists sit, and how native expertise is shared.
Plan succession: every lead, including you, has a named person being prepared.
Stay able to read designs, ask the hard question and judge risk. You do not need to be the best engineer.
Pair with your PE or senior TLs: they own the technical strategy, you fund it and remove obstacles.
Review operational health monthly: crashes, incidents, release cadence, tech-debt list.
Send leadership a short monthly report: delivery, quality, people, risks, requests.
Bring options with a recommendation, never a bare problem.
Build working relationships with product, design, QA, backend, data and HR heads.
Represent mobile in budget discussions: tooling, device labs, CI capacity, vendor SDK costs.
Continuing to act as the TL and taking critical-path code.
Becoming a message relay with no opinion of your own.
Avoiding the underperformance conversation until the team loses trust.
Hiring in a hurry and lowering the bar.
Promising dates to leadership without the team's estimate.

lessons.title: Handling the lead role: situations at each level

blocks.text: The same situation calls for a different response at each level: the TL acts inside the team, the PE acts through the leads, and the EM acts on people and structure.
**The first months as a new TL**

items: You are now leading former peers. Say openly what changes (you decide priorities and technical direction) and what does not (you still code and still take review comments).
Ask each engineer what they want from a lead and what frustrates them today.
Earn authority through fairness and consistency: the same review standard for everyone, including yourself.
Delegate real ownership within the first month. Hand over a module, state the outcome you expect, and let the owner choose the approach.
Decide how decisions are made: discuss openly, then you decide if there is no agreement, and everyone commits.

rows: Two engineers disagree on a design
Ask each for a short written comparison against agreed criteria; decide within days; record the decision
Step in only if it affects several teams; supply the principle or standard that settles it
Stay out of the technical choice; act if the disagreement becomes personal
A project is going to miss its date
Raise it at once with options: cut scope, add time, or phase the release
Check whether the cause is systemic (architecture, dependency, tooling) and fix that
Renegotiate the commitment with product and leadership; shield the team from blame
A senior engineer resists your direction
Listen for the valid point; adopt it if it is right; otherwise explain the reasoning and ask for commitment
Convince with data and a prototype; you have no authority to rely on
Treat persistent refusal as a performance topic in 1:1s
Give specific feedback, pair, reduce task size; tell the EM early with examples
Offer mentoring if the gap is technical; give honest input to the EM
Own it: expectations, improvement plan, weekly review, outcome
State the risk and its cost; offer a safer option with a date; record the debt if overruled
Set the rule for what may never be shortcut: payments, data loss, security
Back the TL; escalate if risk acceptance is above the team's authority
Too many meetings, no coding time
Block focus hours; delegate meetings to engineers as growth opportunities
Choose the few forums where your presence changes the outcome
Fix the meeting load for the whole team
A strong engineer wants to leave
Tell the EM at once; find out the real reason
Offer a harder technical problem or mentorship
Hold a stay conversation; act on growth, scope or pay where you can
Assign a buddy, a starter task and a first production change in week one
Own the 30-60-90 plan and check in at each mark

blocks.text: **How a PE works with Tech Leads**

items: Treat TLs as your primary customers. Your standards succeed only if TLs adopt them.
Hold a monthly mobile leads forum: review RFCs, share incidents, agree standards.
Coach TLs on design and on writing; review their design docs early, before positions harden.
Let the TL decide inside the team. Intervene only on cross-team impact or serious risk, and explain why.
Agree the split in writing: the TL owns how the work is built; the EM owns who, when and why.
Give TLs context from leadership early so that they can plan.
Review each TL on team outcomes: delivery, quality, growth of their engineers.
Coach first-time TLs on delegation and feedback, the two skills they most often lack.
Never overrule a TL in front of their team. Disagree in private.

lessons.title: The mobile organisation in the bigger picture

blocks.text: A mobile org at scale rests on eight pillars. As TL you run them for one team; as PE you set the standard for all teams and find the weakest one.

rows: Modular codebase with clear feature boundaries; teams can work without colliding; a defined Flutter–native boundary
Build time, module coupling, merge conflicts per week
A small platform group owns networking, analytics, design system, navigation and the app shell

Every PR is built and tested automatically; signing and store upload are scripted
PR-to-merge time, CI duration, flaky test rate
Fixed release train, staged rollouts, feature flags, a tested rollback and hotfix path
Release frequency, hotfixes per release, lead time from merge to production
Test pyramid with unit, widget and a small end-to-end suite on critical flows; device coverage for the real user base
Crash-free users and sessions, ANR rate, escaped defects
Budgets for app start, frame rendering, app size and network use, checked in CI

blocks.text: Three cross-cutting concerns sit on top of the pillars:

items: **Team shape.** Feature teams aligned to business areas, supported by a platform team. Decide who owns each module and write it down.
**Contracts with backend.** API versioning, backward compatibility for old app versions, and a forced-upgrade policy. Old app versions stay in users' hands for months.
**Cost of low-end devices and poor networks.** A large share of Indian users are on budget Android phones and variable connectivity. Design and test for them first.

blocks.text: A TL needs working depth in every area below for one app; a PE needs to set the standard in each and be the expert in two or three; an EM needs enough to judge risk and ask the right question.

Take the incidents nobody understands. Root-causing them teaches more than feature work.
Read other teams' design docs and code, including backend.

blocks.text: A fixed release train with objective gates removes most release-day stress. The cadence below is a common pattern for a weekly or fortnightly train; adjust the days to your own.

items: **Continuous merge.** Features merge to main behind flags, off by default. Main is always releasable.
**Branch cut.** On a fixed day, cut the release branch. Anything not merged waits for the next train. No exceptions for features.
**Stabilisation.** Only fixes for regressions enter the branch, each approved by the release owner and merged to main first.
**Regression.** Automated suite plus manual passes on critical flows: login, search, cart, checkout, payment, order tracking.
**Internal and beta.** Distribute to employees and a beta group for at least one to two days.
**Submission.** Submit to App Store and Play with release notes and phased release enabled.
**Staged rollout.** Widen in steps such as 1% → 5% → 20% → 50% → 100%, holding at each step long enough to gather meaningful data.
**Flag ramp.** Turn new features on by percentage, separately from the binary rollout.
**Close.** Tag the release, record the metrics, and note anything to improve.

rows: Below the previous release by more than the agreed margin
Above the previous release or approaching the store's bad-behaviour threshold
API error rate from the new version

items: Release owner: rotates among engineers each train; runs the checklist and decides on gates.
TL: approves cherry-picks and accepts the risk for the team's features.
PE: owns the process design, the tooling and the gate definitions for all teams.
EM: makes sure the rotation is staffed and fair, and that the train is respected by product.
You cannot roll back a binary. Protection comes from flags, kill switches, server-side config and a fast hotfix path.
Store review adds delay. Keep an expedited-review request ready for emergencies on iOS.
Old versions live for months. Backend changes must keep supporting them or trigger a forced upgrade.

blocks.text: In a production incident the order is fixed: stop the damage first, find the cause second, prevent the repeat third. Most incidents go badly because people start debugging before they mitigate.

rows: Users cannot order or pay, data loss, security breach, or crash on launch for many users
Checkout fails on the new version
Immediate, all hours; incident commander named; leadership informed
A major feature is broken or a large segment is affected, with a workaround
One payment method fails; offers not applied
Same day; fix or mitigation within hours
Limited impact or cosmetic on a key screen
Wrong label on one device type

items: **Detect and confirm.** Check the alert against a second source: crash dashboard, funnel metrics, support tickets, your own device.
**Declare.** Assign a severity, open one incident channel, name one incident commander. One person decides.
**Measure the blast radius.** Which app versions, OS versions, devices, cities, user segments, and since when.
**Mitigate.** Use the fastest safe lever, in this order: turn off the feature flag, change remote config, roll back the backend change, halt the staged rollout, then a hotfix build.
**Communicate.** Post updates at a fixed interval, for example every 30 minutes for SEV1: impact, current action, next update time. Brief support with a customer message.
**Find the cause.** Ask what changed: app release, flag, config, backend deploy, third-party SDK, OS update, certificate expiry. Reproduce it.
**Fix.** Make the smallest change that removes the cause. Two reviewers. Add a test that fails without the fix.
**Verify.** Test on the affected devices and versions, plus regression on the surrounding flow.
**Ship the hotfix.** Branch from the release tag, not from main. Request expedited review on iOS. Roll out in stages even under pressure. Consider a forced upgrade if the broken version is dangerous.
**Monitor.** Watch the same metrics until they return to baseline, and confirm in the channel.
**Review.** Within about five working days hold a blameless review: timeline, cause, what slowed detection or mitigation, actions with owners and dates.
**Prevent.** Close the actions: a test, an alert, a flag, a checklist item or a design change.
Do not refactor in a hotfix.
Do not skip review or staged rollout. A bad hotfix is a second incident.
Keep people out of the channel who are not needed, and keep debugging talk in a separate thread.
Write the timeline as you go. Memory is unreliable after the event.
Merge the fix to main the same day so that the next release does not reintroduce the bug.

rows: Incident commander for the team's area; decides the mitigation; assigns one engineer to mitigate and one to investigate
Joins SEV1s and cross-team incidents; leads diagnosis when the cause spans app, backend and SDKs; challenges risky fixes
Handles communication to leadership, product and support; gets people and approvals; protects the engineers from interruptions
Often debugging and reviewing the fix
Writes the incident review; closes team actions
Finds the pattern across incidents; changes architecture, tooling or standards to remove the class of bug

Fewer incidents of the same class across the org

blocks.text: Debugging is a method: form a hypothesis, design the cheapest test that could disprove it, and narrow the search by half each time. Senior engineers are faster because they follow the method, and because they have seen more failure patterns.

items: **State the problem precisely.** Expected result, actual result, who is affected, since when.
**Reproduce it.** Same app version, OS, device class, account state, network condition and flag values. If you cannot reproduce, add logging and narrow from production data.
**Ask what changed.** Releases, flags, config, backend deploys, SDK versions, OS updates.
**Bisect.** Halve the search space each step: by commit with `git bisect`, by flag, by layer (UI, state, repository, network, backend), by device or version.
**Read the evidence before the code.** Full stack trace, breadcrumbs, logs, network trace, the exact request and response.
**One hypothesis, one change.** Write the hypothesis down, predict the result, test, record the outcome.
**Find the root cause.** Ask why until you reach something you can change so that the bug cannot return.
**Fix, then prove it.** A test that fails before and passes after; check the same pattern elsewhere in the code.
**Share it.** A short note on the cause and how you found it trains the whole team.

rows: Xcode debugger, LLDB, view hierarchy debugger
DevTools performance and CPU profiler, frame timeline
Instruments: Time Profiler, Hangs, App Launch

blocks.text: Keep a running record from today: date, what you did, the result, and who can vouch for it. Promotion documents are written from this record.

items: **Staying the best coder.** Taking every hard task yourself makes you the bottleneck and stops the team from growing.
**Waiting to be asked.** Nobody assigns leadership work to an SSE. You take it, with your manager's knowledge.
**Invisible work.** Impact that is not written down and shared does not count at promotion time.
**Rewrites as strategy.** Large rewrites and framework migrations rarely pay back. Prefer incremental migration with measurable steps.
**Technology for its own sake.** A proposal without a business measure will lose to one that has it.
**Avoiding hard conversations.** Late feedback and unspoken disagreement cost more than the discomfort of raising them early.
**No sponsor.** At PE level you need a senior leader who argues for you in rooms you are not in.
**Spreading too thin.** Many side projects reduce the depth of evidence in your main role. Protect focus on the work that builds the case.
**Skipping the people skills.** TL and PE both fail more often on communication and trust than on technical ability.
